newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan excludes China from economic zone plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan excludes China from economic zone plan.

text.p: Taiwan will initially exclude rival China from a planned special zone that will allow unfettered economic activities by foreign investors, the state-funded Central News Agency reported on Thursday.

Soon after the decision, President Lee Teng-hui reiterated his concern about investors' eagerness to invest in communist China and urged enterprises to roll their money back into Taiwan instead of the island's long-time adversary.

"With increasing Taiwan funds flowing into mainland China and decreasing investments in Taiwan, this ultimately will cause a hollowing-out of (Taiwan) industry," Lee told a closed meeting of the ruling Nationalist Party.
"The situation is very disturbing," Lee was quoted by the Central News Agency as saying.
Lee said in August that Taiwan should review its policy of targeting communist China as a main market to avoid depending too heavily on its investment opportunities.
The planned special economic zone, where free exchanges in personnel, information, liquidity and goods will be allowed, will be open to foreign countries but not to China, the agency said.

It said the government's decision was made at a closed-door meeting of officials from Taiwan's main bodies for economic planning and China affairs, the Council for Economic Planning and Development and the Mainland Affairs Council.
The council had objected to the inclusion of China in the special economic zone plan, the agency said.
The United Evening News quoted unidentified officials as saying the council felt the original plan to include China was too "idealistic".
That plan made Taiwan more liberal and international than even Hong Kong and Singapore, council members concluded.
Taiwan should not adopt such complete openness toward China for 15 or 20 years, the agency quoted them as saying.
The Mainland Affairs Council would decide when to welcome China into the special economic zone, the reports said.
Officials were not immediately available for comment.
Taiwan has banned direct contact with China since the Chinese civil war separated them in 1949. All economic activities with China must be conducted through a third region, usually Hong Kong.
Although all investments in China must be government approved, Taiwan remains concerned its economy may become too dependent on China, and thus politically vulnerable.
Taiwan officials, including Lee, regularly accuse China of using commerce as a political lever against the island, and have urged local businesses to slow their mainland investments.

Despite the ban on direct links, indirect commerce has flourished since the late 1980s when political tensions started to thaw. Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$20 billion into China so far.
The island has hoped the special economic zone would help Taiwan fulfil its ambition to become a regional operations hub for Asia-Pacific transnational companies.
